A `{req}` declaration MAY list `:impl:` and `:test:` options, and an `{example}`
declaration MAY list `:test:` options, immediately after its opening fence and
before its body, one project file path per option line. Each anchor MUST be an `{impl}` or `{test}` edge, under
{cite}`requirements.references.targets`, from the definition to the complete
anchored file, for files that cannot or should not carry a reference themselves.
Paths MUST follow the path rules in {cite}`requirements.ci.schema`. Option lines
MUST NOT form part of the definition's text for evidence comparison or for
requirements inputs, and MUST NOT render as body text.

An anchored file MUST be covered by the definition's evidence under
{cite}`requirements.references.evidence_coverage`, by an input containing the
complete file, so changing the file makes that evidence stale. A path that does
not resolve to a readable, permitted file MUST be a validation error naming the
definition and the path; authoring MUST report it before inference, because the
definition cannot be assessed without it. Any other option line in a `{req}` or
`{example}` declaration MUST be a validation error.

Agents SHOULD NOT anchor a file when a more precise reference is available, such
as a reference attached to the Rust item that implements or tests the
definition. Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST give this direction.
rationale:
**Verdict:** the sources satisfy `requirements.references.anchors`. I found no unmarked implementation and no untested obligation. I did not trace the author command to confirm it calls `prepare` before any model call. I relied on `prepare` returning the error, which `unreadable_or_denied_anchors_fail_before_inference` exercises.

**Parsing and syntax**
- `definition_blocks` and `option_line` in `src/lib.rs` read option lines only immediately after the opening fence of `{req}` and `{example}` blocks, one path per line. Both are marked `{impl}`.
- `DefinitionBlock` and `DefinitionOption` in `src/lib.rs` hold the parsed options. Both are marked `{impl}`.
- `collect_definitions` in `src/evidence.rs` accepts `:impl:` and `:test:` on requirements and `:test:` only on examples. Every other option, and an empty path, is a validation error naming the definition and line.
- `anchor_options_are_metadata_not_body_text` tests the parsing. It checks that only lines directly after the fence count, and that `:impl:` text later in the body stays literal.
- `unsupported_and_empty_options_are_validation_errors` tests the error cases, including `:impl:` on an example.

**Option lines excluded from text and rendering**
- `without_options` strips option lines from definition text and from the raw lines used for requirements inputs. It is used in `collect_definitions` and `preprocess_book`.
- `replace_definitions` renders from `text_start`, so option lines do not appear as body text.
- `requirements_inputs_omit_option_lines`, `anchor_options_are_metadata_not_body_text` and `every_definition_gets_a_nested_detail_page_without_an_index` assert this.

**Edge semantics and path rules**
- Anchors are carried as `Anchor` values on `Declaration`. `Anchor::complete_file` resolves them through `read_project_file`, which enforces the same permitted-path rules as other inputs (`requirements.ci.input_containment`). It rejects empty paths and empty files.
- `Anchor::selector` builds a whole-file range, lines 1 to N.
- `DefinitionEdges::current` in `src/index.rs` treats anchors as `{impl}` or `{test}` edges. `DefinitionEdges::group` places them in the matching group. `requirements.index.detail_format` names this grouping explicitly, and `group` carries that marker.
- The `references` tool in `src/authoring/tools.rs` reports anchors as whole-file sites with a null line. It is tested by `references_report_anchors_as_whole_file_sites`, including omission of a denied file.

**Evidence coverage and staleness**
- `validate_references` requires an evidence input that contains the complete anchored file (line 1 through the last line). The error names the evidence file, the file and the definition.
- It reports an unresolvable anchor with the definition, its source location and the path.
- It also counts a test anchor toward an example's required `{test}` reference.
- `anchored_files_must_be_completely_covered_and_resolvable` tests a partial range, a missing file, passing once the range is complete, and staleness after the file changes.

**Authoring before inference**
- `AssessmentSources::prepare` in `src/authoring/inputs.rs` adds one whole-file input per anchor. It fails with `<definition>: cannot read :<kind>: anchor <path>: …` before any inference.
- `unreadable_or_denied_anchors_fail_before_inference` tests both a missing file and a file denied by `habeas.toml`.
- `anchored_files_contribute_complete_file_inputs` checks that the inputs are whole-file and that the subject text excludes the option lines.

**Skill direction**
- `assets/skills/habeas-requirements/SKILL.md` (line 58) tells agents not to anchor a file when a more precise reference, such as a comment on a Rust item, is available. The requirement itself anchors this file with `:impl:`, and the supplied evidence covers lines 1–70.

**Marking**
- Every anchor-handling function I found is marked `{impl}`, including `Declaration`, `Anchor`, `complete_file`, `selector`, `collect_definitions`, `validate_references`, `current`, `prepare`, `references`, `preprocess_book`, `replace_definitions`, `definition_blocks`, `option_line` and `without_options`. I found no extra unspecified behavior and no acknowledged FIXME gaps.

Project text files MAY use the `{impl}`, `{cite}`, and `{test}` roles with a backtick-delimited full requirement or example name. Each reference is a directed edge between its source and the named definition. A source is a project source item or a requirement or example declaration. `{cite}` MUST mean that the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition, and is an edge from the source to the definition. `{impl}` MUST mean that the source implements part of the definition: it makes a decision, performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case that the definition specifies. A requirement MAY implement part of another requirement by refining one of its obligations. Calling code that implements a definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, MUST NOT by itself count as implementing it. A requirement stating a convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the source that carries out the convention as a whole, such as the step that collects and reports those outputs. `{test}` MUST mean that the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies: a test through its scenario and the assertions about that scenario's outcome, or a named example through the concrete case it describes. `{impl}` and `{test}` are edges from the definition to the source. Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the definitions it implements or tests. Habeas MUST find these references throughout project source files and MUST fail with the source file and line if a name has no matching `{req}` or `{example}` definition. In Markdown, escaped roles and roles in code examples MUST remain literal. Evidence snapshots and generated build output MUST NOT be counted as additional source references.

A requirement or example evidence file at `evidence/<full-name>.json` MUST be a JSON object with exactly `requirement` or `example`, `determination`, `rationale`, and `inputs`. The definition text and rationale MUST be nonempty strings, `determination` MUST use one of the outcomes defined by {cite}`requirements.ci.outcomes`, and `inputs` MUST be an array. Every evidence input MUST have exactly one of four forms: a file-range input with `file`, `line_start`, `line_end`, and `text`; a Rust-item input with `rust_file`, `rust_item`, and `text`; a requirements input with `requirements`, `matches`, and `text`; or a definition input with `definition` and `text`. File paths MUST resolve to permitted inputs under {cite}`requirements.ci.input_containment`. Project-local paths SHOULD be recorded relative to the project for portability; absolute and parent-relative paths MAY be used when their resolved targets are permitted. Line numbers MUST be positive integers, `matches` MUST be an array of distinct full definition names, and `text` MUST be a nonempty array of strings.

For every `{impl}` and `{test}` reference in a project source file, including one in a requirement or example declaration, the evidence file for the referenced requirement or example MUST contain an input whose resolved source ranges cover the reference's file and line. A `{cite}` reference MUST NOT require coverage; it is discoverable through {cite}`requirements.authoring.reference_index`. Habeas MUST report every uncovered reference with its role, full name, source file, and line number.

description: Design and vet requirements and examples for user-visible behavior changes in a Habeas mdBook project before coding; maintain definitions and references.

When a user requests new or changed user-visible behavior in a Habeas project, first read the relevant requirements, code, and tests. Identify requirements that already express the intended behavior. For gaps, draft the smallest set of observable obligations, including important outcomes and failure cases, without committing to an implementation.

Run `habeas info <selection>` to read current requirement and named example texts, evidence states, rationales, inputs, and validation findings as Markdown. A selection is a full name, which selects exactly, or a glob where `*` matches any number of characters, including dots, when you need to inspect a group.

Show the user the full IDs and text of existing requirements to reuse, plus the proposed chapter location, full IDs, and exact fenced text of any additions or changes. State open product choices separately. Ask the user to agree to or revise this requirement set. User-provided exact requirement text or explicit agreement earlier in the conversation counts as approval; a general request to build the feature does not. Keep drafts out of the mdBook while review is pending, and do not write implementation or test code yet.

After agreement, install the approved requirements in the mdBook and confirm their names. Then implement the behavior and add tests and traceability references. Run `habeas author --all` to create or refresh evidence through the configured model. The supervising agent must not compose evidence JSON, rationales, determinations, or source snapshots itself or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If implementation reveals a substantive change to an approved obligation, review and install the revised requirement before coding that change. Missing or false evidence is expected while implementation is incomplete.

The authoring harness assesses whether the code marked `{impl}` for a requirement implements every obligation completely and exactly as stated, and whether tests cover interesting design cases. It also treats as gaps any code that implements part of the requirement without `{impl}`, including code that only cites it, and any behavior in `{impl}` code that no definition implemented there specifies. When another requirement implements part of the subject, it checks only that the text carries out that part. For absent tests, it assesses whether simplicity or impracticality justifies their absence. For an example, it assesses whether test setup and assertions cover the scenario and expected outcomes. Use these criteria while implementing and fixing reported gaps; leave evidence judgments and rationales to the harness.

Requirement and example judgments have three outcomes: `true`, `false`, or `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}`. The harness uses FIXME when source comments or tests explicitly acknowledge the uncovered aspects, recording their issue references or other identifying content. A documented gap does not excuse other, unacknowledged gaps. Use the `habeas-evidence` skill for the authoring workflow.

Inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Check that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, mark every requirement implemented at the relevant point with `{impl}` and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A reference alone does not explain why a behavior, such as accepting `^C`, is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference in an attached Rust comment or within its body, including trait methods and test helpers. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions, and there is no uncited-function waiver. If no existing requirement explains an internal helper, propose a requirement scoped to that area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all, get the user's agreement, and mark the helper with `{impl}`. That requirement's review checks that it explains each implementing function. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior.

Put requirements in the book's Markdown source directory. Define each with a fenced `{req}` directive: the opening line is three or more colons followed by `{req} name`, and the closing line has at least as many colons. Derive the full name from the chapter path relative to that directory: remove `.md`, change `/` to `.`, and append the directive name. For nested chapters, omit a leading `reqs/` and a trailing `/index` or `/README`.
Pressing q MUST stop managed forwards.

Everything between the fences is the requirement body, including headings and diagrams. Use a longer outer colon fence when the body contains a nested colon directive. Use BCP 14 terms when stating obligations.

Write a concrete case as a separate `{example}` directive with the same chapter-qualified naming and fence rules. Reference at least one requirement it illustrates from the example body: `{test}` when the example is a case the requirement's review should check, `{cite}` when the requirement is context for the example's own review, or both. A true example determination needs test references and an evidence rationale explaining how the tests cover its interesting aspects. Keep names unique across requirements and examples.
Use fully qualified names for implementation, citation, and test references. Place them on the relevant source or book line:
Choose the role by what the source does:

- `{impl}`: it implements part of the definition, making a decision, performing a check, producing an output, or handling a case the definition specifies. Calling code that implements the definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, does not count. A requirement that refines another's obligation can `{impl}` it. A convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the code that carries it out as a whole.
- `{test}`: it is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies, through a test's scenario and assertions or an example's concrete case. Incidental setup does not count.
- `{cite}`: it relies on, supports, or refers to the definition without implementing or testing it.

`{impl}` and `{test}` make the source an input to the definition's assessment and must be covered by its evidence. `{cite}` makes the cited definition context for the citing requirement or example, needs no coverage, and does not count toward the cited requirement's implementation.

When a file that implements or tests a requirement cannot or should not carry a reference itself, such as a shipped skill, a stylesheet copied into other projects, or a README, anchor it from the declaration with `:impl: <path>` or `:test: <path>` option lines directly after the opening fence (examples accept only `:test:`). An anchor covers the whole file, so do not anchor a file when a more precise reference is available, such as a comment attached to the Rust item that implements or tests the requirement.

When a requirement or example changes, run `habeas author --all`, then the Cargo tests. Address reported implementation, test, or reference gaps and rerun the harness. Validation itself checks stored evidence without inference.

name with the `{term}` role; the book renders the phrase as a plain link, without

named definition has no evidence record of its own and cannot substitute for a
requirement citation. Dependent evidence snapshots its complete declaration;
review changes to phrases and bodies because they invalidate that evidence.

`habeas mdbook` MUST generate one evidence detail page for every requirement and
named example defined in a rendered chapter, whether or not the book contains a
requirements index. Each page MUST be a subchapter nested under the chapter that
defines it, in definition order, titled by the definition's full name, at a path
derived from that chapter's path. Books configured by {cite}`requirements.cli.setup`
fold these subchapters in the sidebar until a reader expands their chapter.

The requirements index MUST show each requirement's evidence state as Valid, Missing, Determination false, FIXME, or Invalid. Valid MUST mean its determination is true and its record passes the same evidence and reference coverage checks as `habeas::validate()`. A false or FIXME determination MUST have its distinct state when the record passes all other checks. The FIXME state MUST pass validation while retaining its distinct label. Malformed or stale evidence MUST remain Invalid regardless of its determination. Each detail page MUST show any validation findings.

Each evidence detail page MUST display its state as a Shields.io static badge image with meaningful alt text and the current requirement or example body as a Markdown block quote labeled by kind. It MUST render the recorded rationale as Markdown in a Rationale section and display the recorded FIXME strings when the determination is FIXME. Inputs MUST be grouped under headings in this order: Implementation, for sources reached by an `{impl}` edge from the definition, including anchored files; Tests, for sources reached by a `{test}` edge, including tests, examples, and anchored files; Referenced definitions, for declarations the definition cites and their terminology; and Other sources, for the remaining inputs the assessment consulted. Edges MUST be determined from the current references under {cite}`requirements.references.targets` and {cite}`requirements.references.anchors`. Each group and each input MUST be a collapsible disclosure element, with groups expanded and inputs collapsed by default, so readers can move between groups and open individual sources. Each input MUST have its own subsection identifying its selector. A file-range or Rust-item input MUST show its resolved file and inclusive line range. A requirements input MUST show its selection and each matched definition's full name, file, and inclusive line range. Each subsection MUST show the exact recorded text in a fenced code block. Code fences MUST request Rust highlighting for `.rs` files and language-aware highlighting for Markdown, JSON, TOML, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, and Python files; TOML MAY use INI highlighting when native TOML highlighting is unavailable.

Each requirement and example definition badge MUST link to its evidence detail page, and each rendered requirement and example MUST be followed by a "See evidence" link to that page. Each detail page MUST link back to the definition's anchored badge and, when an index exists, to the index. Reference badges MUST continue to link to the definition. These links MUST resolve when a requirement name contains `.md`, as in `requirements.cli.mdbook`.

When `output.html.git-repository-url` names a GitHub repository and `output.html.edit-url-template` uses that repository's `/edit/<branch>/{path}` form, each safely resolved source location displayed for an evidence input MUST link its repository-relative file and inclusive line range to `/blob/<branch>/<file>#L<start>-L<end>`. A source location MUST remain plain text when a safe URL cannot be derived. A generated detail page MUST use its evidence JSON file as the mdBook edit target when the file exists, or its requirement chapter when the evidence file is missing.
